body_ar:
درج كثير من العلماء في العصور المتأخرة على إطلاق كلمة (ذات الله) على ما يقابل صفاته سبحانه وتعالى، وهذا المعنى غير معروف في لسان العرب ولا في المصطلحات الشرعية، ولا تضاف كلمة (ذات) إلى الأعلام إلا شذوذاً، والأصل أن تضاف إلى غير الأعلام كالإله فيقال: (ذات الإله) كما كانت مستعملة في الجاهلية وفي صدر الإسلام، ويقصد بها عند من أطلقها منهم أنها ملته وشرعته وسبيله، لا بمعنى ما يقابل الصفة كما يطلقها المتأخرون.
إطلاق لفظ (الذات) على الله عز وجل:
قال شيخنا حفظه الله: [ يقال نفسه كما قال كتب ربكم الآية أما من نسب ذاتاً له فقد عنى التي له ملته شرعته سبيله والأصل أن تضاف للإله لا للضمير أو للفظ لله كمثل ما قال خبيب إذ صلب وقال النابغة الذبياني، الذرب لأنها تأنيث ذي الملتزمِ فيه الإضافة لغير العلمِ لظاهر قال ابن مالك وقد ذكر ما يلزم (ذو) في ذا الصدد ذو ذات أنثاه ذوات الجمع وجريان الأصل مثل الفرع نعم أتت مضافةً لله في كذبات القانت الأواه وهو شذوذ ونظيره ذو بكة مما وجهه الشذوذ] هذه الأبيات كلها في مبحث واحد، وهو مبحث إطلاق الذات على الله سبحانه وتعالى...
body_en:
*[Site synopsis]* Many scholars of the later ages have taken to applying the phrase "the essence of God" (dhāt Allāh) to what stands over against His attributes, glorified and exalted is He. This sense is not known in the speech of the Arabs, nor in the technical vocabulary of the revealed law. The word "dhāt" is not annexed to proper names except anomalously; the rule is that it be annexed to what is not a proper name, such as "al-Ilāh", so that one says "dhāt al-Ilāh" — as it was in use in the age of ignorance and in the first period of Islam. Those among them who used it meant by it His religion, His revealed way and His path, and not the sense of what stands over against an attribute, in which the later scholars apply it.

## Applying the word "al-dhāt" to God, mighty and majestic

Our Sheikh, may God preserve him, said:

*[One says "His self", as He said, "Your Lord has prescribed…" — the verse. But whoever ascribes a dhāt to Him has meant that which is His: His religion, His revealed way, His path. The rule is that it be annexed to "al-Ilāh", not to a pronoun nor to the word "Allāh" — as in what Khubayb said when he was crucified, and what al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani, the sharp-tongued, said — because it is the feminine of "dhū", in which annexation to what is not a proper name is obligatory, on the apparent sense of what Ibn Malik said when he mentioned what "dhū" requires in this respect: "dhū"; "dhāt" is its feminine; "dhawāt" the plural; and the base form runs as the derived form does. Yes — it did come annexed to "Allāh", in the untruths of the devout, oft-sighing one; and that is an anomaly, and its counterpart is "dhū Bakkah", which likewise is to be accounted anomalous.]*

These lines are all on a single topic, the topic of applying "al-dhāt" to God, glorified and exalted is He …

The opening paragraph is a synopsis written by the site, speaking about the lesson in the third person; everything from the section heading onward is the lecturer's own words as transcribed, together with the quoted lines of the versified base text, which are his teacher's. flags.arabic: قال شيخنا حفظه الله في منظومته في الأسماء والصفات
flags.context: the formula introducing each quoted line of the versified base text in this series

flags.note: Record 734 of this series settles the referent in a way the creed run (IDs 707-721) did not: it has 'قال شيخنا حفظه الله في منظومته في الأسماء والصفات' — 'OUR Sheikh, may God preserve him, said in his versification on the names and attributes'. The first-person plural possessive makes the author the lecturer's own teacher, living at the time of the lesson, and the base text a versification devoted specifically to the divine names and attributes. Elsewhere in the series the shorter 'قال الشيخ' and 'يقول الشيخ' are used for the same person. The author is nowhere named. Note that this is a different base text from the versified creed expounded in records 707-721, which record 719 identifies as a versification of the Mukhtaṣar of Khalil.

flags.arabic: the whole of the quoted verse passage
flags.context: nine lines of grammatical verse on the annexation of ذات, quoted with no commentary
options: render as prose in italics, provisionally, and obtain the full lesson before publication
render and present as settled
withhold the record
flags.note: The hardest passage in this slice, and the English must be treated as provisional throughout. It is a technical argument in Arabic grammar — that 'ذات' is the feminine of 'ذو', that 'ذو' must be annexed to a common noun and not a proper name, and that annexing 'ذات' to the name 'Allāh' is therefore anomalous — conducted entirely in verse, with elliptical references to Khubayb ibn Adi, to al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani, to Ibn Malik's Alfiyyah and to a report about Abraham. None of the four is explained, because the explanation is precisely what the record breaks off before giving. Several renderings below are best guesses and are flagged individually. This record should not be published from this draft alone; the .doc behind the download is needed.

flags.arabic: نعم أتت مضافةً لله في كذبات القانت الأواه
flags.context: the counter-example admitted in the verse
options: it did come annexed to "Allāh", in the untruths of the devout, oft-sighing one
it did come annexed to God, in the lies of the devout, oft-sighing one
it occurred in annexation to Allāh in the matter of the three sayings of Abraham
flags.note: Two difficulties in half a line. 'القانت الأواه' is an allusion to Abraham, built from two Qur'anic descriptions of him (Sūrat al-Naḥl 16:120 and Sūrat al-Tawbah 9:114), and the verse assumes the reader knows it; the English keeps the epithets and does not name him, as the Arabic does not. 'كذبات' refers to the well-known report of the three occasions of Abraham's speech, two of which the report itself describes as 'في ذات الله' — which is exactly the annexation the verse is admitting as a counter-example. The English word 'lies' predicated of a prophet reads far harder in English than 'كذبات' does in the Arabic of the report; 'untruths' has been used, and the choice is flagged rather than made silently. Style guide section 12.

flags.arabic: ونظيره ذو بكة مما وجهه الشذوذ
flags.context: the second counter-example in the verse
options: its counterpart is "dhū Bakkah", which likewise is to be accounted anomalous
its like is "dhū Bakkah", whose explanation is anomaly
read a place-name or a title not recoverable from the served text
flags.note: 'بكة' is a name of Mecca (Sūrat Āl ʿImrān 3:96), and the phrase is offered as a second instance of 'ذو' annexed to a proper name, which the rule forbids. But the referent of 'ذو بكة' is not given, the phrase is not otherwise common, and the commentary that would have identified it is exactly what the record loses. Rendered literally and flagged.

flags.arabic: كمثل ما قال خبيب إذ صلب
flags.context: the first illustration in the verse
options: as in what Khubayb said when he was crucified
supply the verse of Khubayb that is meant
flags.note: Khubayb ibn Adi is the Companion executed at Mecca, whose lines spoken before his death are well known and include the phrase 'في ذات الإله' — which is why he is cited here, as an early witness to the annexation the verse is defending. The verse does not quote him and the English does not supply the quotation. Same for al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani, the pre-Islamic poet, cited with the epithet 'الذرب', rendered 'the sharp-tongued'; that epithet may equally be the poet's own known by-name or a metrical filler, and it has been rendered rather than dropped.

flags.arabic: ما يقابل صفاته / ما يقابل الصفة
flags.context: the site's synopsis, twice, on the later usage of dhāt
options: what stands over against His attributes
that which is opposed to the attributes
the essence as distinct from the attributes
flags.note: This is what the record is about and the English must not settle it. The claim is that the later scholars' use of 'ذات' — the essence as the correlate of the attributes, which is the standard technical vocabulary of kalām and the vocabulary used in record 738 of this same series — is unknown to the Arabs and to the revealed law. 'Stands over against' has been used rather than 'is distinct from' because the Arabic 'يقابل' names a correlation and does not itself assert a real distinction, which is the point in dispute. A reader must be able to see that the record is objecting to a usage, not settling a doctrine, and that it never says what should be said instead — the commentary that would have said so is missing.

translator_notes: One of a run of fourteen records, IDs 734-747, the series 'The Names and Attributes', all built to the same template and all excerpts. Each carries a site-written synopsis, then a section heading, then the opening formula and the first lines of a lesson, and then breaks off on an ellipsis; the full text sits behind a .doc download in the /medias/doc/esmawesivat-* series, numbered 1 to 14 in the same order as the IDs. None of the SEF aliases in this run carries a timestamp, so no upload date can be read from them.

The source's final line, 'تحميل المادة' ('download the material'), is the label of a download link in the page furniture, not part of the text. It is recorded as source_download_link and omitted from body_ar and body_en.
Qur'anic renderings here are interpretive and are not a substitute for the Arabic.

The least usable record in this slice as it stands: nine lines of technical grammatical verse with a single sentence of commentary, which does no more than say what the lines are about before the text stops.

This record's SEF alias ends '737--3.html' although it is the fourth in the series, matching the alias of record 736 ('736--3.html'). The aliases in this run are auto-generated from titles that differ only by a bracketed numeral and are not reliable; the download file name, esmawesivat-4.doc, agrees with the title.

The verse is rendered as continuous prose in italics per style guide section 4; the source runs all nine lines together with no hemistich markers, and no line division has been imposed. No rhymed English has been attempted.
Proper names are given without diacritics in body text per style guide section 2: Khubayb, al-Nabighah al-Dhubyani, Ibn Malik.
No ruling term from the five-rulings table appears anywhere in the record.
